title: A Orchard for the Clock
premise: In 1917 Ohio, Silas Nakamura, a quiet Japanese immigrant who drives for a white suffragist and secretly reads her mail, believes history belongs to other people. When a census taker's probing questions mark him as an 'enemy alien' after America enters the war, he loses his job, his registration papers become a leash, and the town that ignored him turns watchful. His only anchor is a promise made in peacetime to deliver a letter to a German-immigrant orchard keeper across the river — now also declared an enemy. As spring floods threaten to break the ice, Silas must choose between legal safety and keeping his word, discovering that belonging is something you claim, not something you're granted.
about_author: R. M. Okonkwo is the pen name of a former archivist who spent years cataloguing immigrant detention records from the American Midwest. Their fiction excavates the small, unrecorded acts of courage that official histories overlook.

chapters.title: The Weight of Other People's Words
chapters.summary: Silas Nakamura drives Adeline Marsh, a suffragist, through a cold Ohio winter, reading her correspondence each night before delivering it — petitions, threats, love letters. He prides himself on being a man history passes over. POV: Silas. Emotional beat: comfortable invisibility, with a faint ache beneath it.

chapters.title: One Question Too Many
chapters.summary: A census taker arrives at the boarding house and lingers on Silas's entry: birthplace, allegiance, race. His casual questions about 'the German family across the river' unsettle Silas more than the ones about himself. POV: Silas. Emotional beat: first crack in his belief that paperwork is harmless.

chapters.title: The Promise in Peacetime
chapters.summary: Flashback woven into present: months earlier, dying orchard-keeper Heinrich Brandt asked Silas to carry a sealed letter to his estranged son in Cleveland when 'the time comes.' Silas agreed lightly. Now war has been declared, and both Brandts are named enemy aliens. POV: Silas. Emotional beat: guilt of promises made cheaply.

chapters.title: Registration
chapters.summary: Silas reports to the marshal's office as required, fingerprinted and photographed, issued papers he must carry always. Adeline hires him back but warns him to be careful; her allies need no scandal. A neighbor reports 'foreigners' meeting at the Brandt orchard. POV: Silas, with a brief Adeline section. Emotional beat: humiliation sharpening into resolve.

chapters.title: What the Letters Say
chapters.summary: Reading Adeline's mail, Silas finds a government inquiry about 'disloyal elements' among her staff. Someone has reported him. He begins lying — to the postman, to Adeline, to himself — while mapping the route to Cleveland in his head. POV: Silas. Emotional beat: paranoia transforming his gift for reading others into survival.

chapters.title: The Orchard Under Watch
chapters.summary: Silas visits the Brandt orchard at night and finds it half-abandoned, Heinrich's daughter Greta keeping the trees alive alone, men having thrown stones through the greenhouse. She asks nothing of him; he volunteers to take the letter anyway. POV: alternating Silas and Greta. Emotional beat: two outsiders recognizing each other.

chapters.title: Adeline's Choice
chapters.summary: Adeline discovers Silas's plan and confronts him: if he's caught aiding an enemy alien, she loses everything she's built for the vote. But she remembers what it is to be told where women may not go. She gives him her motorcar and one day. POV: Adeline, then Silas. Emotional beat: allyship earned, not owed.

chapters.title: The River Road
chapters.summary: Silas drives toward Cleveland through sleet with the letter hidden in the spare tire well, stopped twice by suspicious deputies who study his face too long. The second stop nearly ends him until a deputy recognizes Adeline's car. POV: Silas. Emotional beat: terror and exhilaration — history is happening to him now.

chapters.title: The Son
chapters.summary: Heinrich's son Emil, serving in the U.S. Army on leave, receives his father's letter: not forgiveness, but the deed to the orchard and a request to keep the family name rooted in American soil. Emil asks Silas why he came. Silas answers honestly: because someone had to. POV: Silas. Emotional beat: the promise kept, and its cost still unknown.

chapters.title: When the Ice Breaks
chapters.summary: Silas returns as the river ice cracks apart in the thaw. The town has learned of his trip; the marshal waits at the boarding house. Adeline stands beside him, Greta behind him, and the deputy's testimony tips the balance. Silas keeps his job, his papers, and something larger: a self no census can define. POV: Silas. Emotional beat: quiet, hard-won belonging.
